title: Design a news feed (Twitter/Instagram)
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, fan-out push/pull/hybrid, feed storage, ranking, counters, deletes. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A news feed shows each user a stream of posts from the people they follow, newest and most relevant first. Twitter/X home timeline, Instagram feed, Facebook News Feed, LinkedIn feed. The famous trick is deciding whether to do the work when someone posts (fan-out on write) or when someone reads (fan-out on read). This note is the full interview version of the Chirp stage in the Master scaling track (stage 6, where a hybrid timeline appears); read that for how it evolves with scale.

Functional requirements

  • Post (text, images, video) and follow/unfollow.
  • Home feed: posts from followees, reverse-chronological or ranked, infinitely scrollable.
  • Likes, comments, reposts; user profile timeline (a user's own posts).
  • Notifications of new activity (optional).

Non-functional requirements

  • Feed load under 200 ms p99 (the main screen of the product).
  • Posting feels instant; followers may see it a few seconds later (eventual consistency is fine).
  • Read-heavy: 100 to 1000 feed reads per post.
  • Highly available; stale feed is acceptable, empty feed is not.
  • Handles celebrities (100M followers) and normal users (200 followers) in one system.

Decision gravity. The push versus pull decision (and the hybrid) shapes data model, cost and latency for years. Wrong choice shows as either massive write amplification (push for celebrities) or slow reads (pull for everyone). Moving later is a major migration.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper: print and deliver a personalised copy to each subscriber's door (push), or have subscribers visit the kiosk and pick articles when they want (pull).

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping into ranking ML before stating the fan-out strategy.
  • Ignoring the celebrity case.
  • Not asking: chronological or ranked? How many followees on average?

notes.title: API
notes.html:
POST /v1/posts
Idempotency-Key: 6d2e-...
{ "text": "hello world", "mediaIds": ["m_81"], "replyTo": null }
201 { "postId": "1853740192837465088", "createdAt": "2026-11-09T10:15:00Z" }

POST /v1/users/u_42/follow        -> 204 (idempotent)
DELETE /v1/users/u_42/follow      -> 204
GET /v1/feed/home?cursor=1853740192837465088&limit=20
200 { "items": [ { "postId":"...", "author":{"id":"u_7","name":"Asha"}, "text":"...",
                   "media":[...], "counts":{"likes":341,"replies":12}, "likedByMe":false } ],
      "nextCursor": "1853740192837400000" }

GET /v1/users/u_7/posts?cursor=...&limit=20      // profile timeline
POST /v1/posts/{id}/like        -> 204 (idempotent)

Pagination is cursor-based using the post id (time-sortable), never OFFSET, because new posts shift offsets and duplicate or skip items. Post ids are Snowflake-style 64-bit integers (timestamp in the high bits) so they sort by time and carry no coordination cost.

Industry example. Twitter's Snowflake id generator (41 bits time, 10 bits machine, 12 bits sequence); Instagram built a similar scheme inside Postgres embedding shard id.

Everyday analogy. A bookmark in the stack of papers: "continue after this one", unaffected by new papers added on top.

Common interview traps.

  • Offset pagination (duplicates and skips as the feed moves).
  • Returning full post bodies for each feed item from the feed store instead of hydrating.
  • Non-idempotent like/follow endpoints.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 300M DAU, each opens the feed 10 times/day, posts 0.5/day on average, follows 200 users, 20% of users post per day.

Quantity Calculation Result
Posts 300M x 0.5 150M/day, 1,700/s avg, peak ~5,000/s
Feed reads 300M x 10 / 86,400 35,000/s avg, peak ~100,000/s
Read:write 35,000 / 1,700 ~20:1 on requests (higher once refresh is counted)
Fan-out on write 150M posts x 200 followers avg 30B feed inserts/day = 350,000/s avg
Feed cache size 300M users x 800 post ids x 8 B ~2 TB (ids only)
Post storage 150M x 1 KB (text+metadata) 150 GB/day, ~55 TB/year (media separate, in object storage)
Celebrity post 100M followers x 1 post 100M inserts for one post

What this tells you. Pushing to 200 followers on average is fine (350k cheap in-memory inserts per second across a cluster); the celebrity case (100M inserts for one tweet) breaks it. Keeping only ids (8 B) in the feed cache makes 2 TB feasible across 30 to 60 Redis nodes at 64 GB each. Media is the real storage and bandwidth cost: serve from a CDN.

Everyday analogy. Delivering 200 newspapers is a normal morning; delivering 100 million at once for a single edition needs a different plan.

Common interview traps.

  • Using average followers and forgetting the long tail.
  • Storing full post JSON in each follower's feed (storage explosion).
  • Not separating media from text storage.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Post service: validates, assigns id, writes to the Posts DB (sharded by author or post id), emits post.created to Kafka (outbox).
  • Social graph service: followers(userId) and following(userId) lists; adjacency in a sharded store (MySQL like Facebook TAO, or Redis/Cassandra); cached.
  • Fan-out workers: consume post.created, look up followers, insert the post id into each follower's feed list.
  • Feed cache: per user Redis sorted set or list of (postId) limited to the latest 500 to 800.
  • Feed service: reads ids from the cache, merges in celebrity posts (pull), hydrates posts (batched MGET), applies ranking and filters (blocked, muted), returns a page.
  • Counters (likes, replies): separate high-throughput counter store; eventually consistent.

Industry examples. Twitter's 2012 timeline architecture: home timelines in Redis (about 800 entries), fan-out on write, with celebrities handled separately; Instagram: Cassandra/Postgres plus caching, move to ranked feed; Facebook: ranked pull-based aggregation of many sources (leaf servers), famously more compute on read because the ranking is personalised.

Decision gravity. Store ids only and hydrate at read time. It decouples the feed from post edits and deletes (the post store is the single source of truth), at the cost of an extra batched read. Reversible and cheap.

Everyday analogy. The feed holds a list of article numbers; the printing office hands you the actual article when you open the paper.

Common interview traps.

  • Copying the post body into every feed (edits and deletes become impossible).
  • One synchronous fan-out inside the post request.
  • Using SQL joins posts JOIN follows at read time at this scale.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read vs hybrid

Fan-out on read (pull). When Asha opens the feed: get her followees (200), fetch recent posts of each (200 queries or one multi-get), merge by time, take top 20. Write is trivial; read is expensive (200 lookups and a merge per open, 100k opens/s = 20M lookups/s).

Fan-out on write (push). When a post is created: look up the author's followers, insert the post id into each follower's feed list. Read is one Redis call (ZREVRANGE). Write amplification equals the follower count.

Hybrid (what Twitter and Instagram settled on). Push for normal authors; for authors above a threshold (for example 100k to 1M followers), do not push. At read time, take the user's precomputed feed (pushed items) and merge in recent posts from the few celebrities that user follows (pull from the celebrity's own timeline, cached heavily).

# Feed read (hybrid)
def home_feed(user, cursor, n=20):
    ids = redis.zrevrangebyscore(f"feed:{user}", cursor, "-inf", start=0, num=n+20)
    for c in celebrity_followees(user):                       # usually under 20
        ids += timeline_cache.recent(c, since=cursor, limit=n)
    ids = sorted(set(ids), reverse=True)[:n]                  # snowflake ids sort by time
    return hydrate(ids)

Additional tricks:

  • Active-user-only fan-out: do not push into feeds of users inactive for 30 days (saves 30 to 50% of work); rebuild their feed lazily when they return (a pull).
  • Batching and priorities: fan-out through Kafka partitions keyed by author; paid or close-friend recipients first.
  • Backpressure: if fan-out lags, the post is still available through pull for the author's profile and the feed is simply slightly stale.

Decision gravity. The follower threshold is a policy knob (reversible per author), but the hybrid read path is a permanent architectural component. Alternative: pure pull with massive caching, which Facebook does for ranked feeds because ranking is computed per request anyway. Hybrid breaks if the pull set per user grows (following many celebrities); cap or rank which celebrities to pull.

Everyday analogy. The mail carrier delivers letters from ordinary senders to your mailbox, but a famous newsletter's issue sits in the lobby for you to pick up.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "push" without addressing celebrities, or "pull" without addressing read cost.
  • Not stating the threshold or how it's decided.
  • Merging at read time without a time-sorted id.

Feed storage and data model

Redis sorted set feed:{userId} with ZADD feed:42 <score=postId> <member=postId> and ZREMRANGEBYRANK feed:42 0 -801 to cap at 800. Memory per entry about 40 to 60 B in a sorted set (use a plain list or a compact encoding for lower, since score and member are the same id; many designs use a list with LPUSH/LTRIM and the time-sorted id embedded).

Sharding: hash userId over Redis nodes (consistent hashing or Redis Cluster with 16,384 slots). Replication: 1 replica; the feed is a cache that can be rebuilt from the graph and posts, so durability is not critical; losing a node means a rebuild by pull for affected users.

Posts DB: sharded by postId or authorId. Author sharding gives cheap profile timelines but creates hot shards for celebrities; id sharding spreads writes but needs scatter for the profile page (served by a secondary index/cache). Instagram chose sharding with the shard id embedded in the 64-bit id. Posts are immutable except edits and deletes; deletes are soft (tombstone), and the hydrator drops tombstoned ids.

CREATE TABLE posts (
  post_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,         -- snowflake
  author_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  body TEXT, media JSONB, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
  deleted BOOLEAN DEFAULT false);
CREATE INDEX posts_by_author ON posts (author_id, post_id DESC);

Decision gravity. Treat the feed cache as derived and rebuildable; do not pay for strong durability. The rebuild path must exist and be fast (hundreds of ms) or a node loss becomes an outage when millions of users miss at once (cache stampede, add jitter and request coalescing).

Everyday analogy. A to-read pile you can rebuild at any time from the newspaper archive.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating Redis feed as the system of record.
  • Rebuilds for millions of users at once without throttling.
  • Unbounded feed length.

Ranking and hydration

Chronological feed: sort by id. Ranked feed (Instagram, Facebook, modern X): two stages.

  1. Candidate generation: the latest 500 candidates from push + pull (+ recommended content).
  2. Ranking: a model scores each candidate (P(like), P(comment), P(dwell)) from features (author affinity, recency, post type, user history), with business rules (diversity, no 5 posts in a row from one author, filter blocked and muted users). Then top N.

Latency budget: 200 ms total: Redis ids 5 ms, hydrate posts 20 ms (batched MGET from a posts cache with 95% hit rate), features 30 ms (feature store), model 50 ms (served from a GPU/CPU model server), counters 10 ms, overhead. Precompute features offline and keep affinity scores in a feature store; cache the final ranked page for 30 to 60 s per user to survive refresh spam.

Hydration is batched: collect all ids, MGET post:{id} from Redis, fetch misses from the DB in one WHERE post_id IN (...), fill the cache. Counters (likes) are read from a separate counter service with a cached value that is a few seconds stale.

Decision gravity. Ranking is policy and highly reversible (A/B test everything), but it commits you to the infrastructure cost (feature store, model serving) and the risk of "filter bubble" and trust issues. Keep a chronological fallback path and a kill switch for the model.

Everyday analogy. An editor choosing which of the 500 stories go on the front page, balancing freshness and what each reader tends to enjoy.

Common interview traps.

  • Ranking inline with a synchronous cold call to the DB per candidate.
  • No fallback when the ranker is down.
  • Ignoring blocked and muted users in the push path (filter at read time too).

Counters, likes and hot posts

Likes arrive at high rates for viral posts (100k likes/s on one post). Counting by UPDATE posts SET likes=likes+1 row-locks a hot row. Instead:

  • Write the like event (user, post) to Kafka and a likes table (dedupe by (user, post) unique key for idempotence).
  • Maintain the counter in Redis with INCR, sharded for hot keys (split into N sub-counters, sum on read), flush periodically to the DB.
  • The displayed count is approximate for hot posts (eventually consistent), exact for "did I like it" (from the likes table/bitmap per user).

Decision gravity. Accepting approximate counters is a product decision that removes the hottest DB row in the system, reversible. Exactness is only required for the user's own state.

Industry example. Facebook TAO caches associations and counts with write-through and eventual consistency; Twitter's counters aggregate asynchronously ("Rainbird"-style, confirm names with current engineering posts).

Everyday analogy. A stadium tally clicker per gate rather than one clicker everyone fights over.

Common interview traps.

  • A single row per post counter updated in place.
  • Letting a duplicate like request increment twice.

Media, deletes and failure handling

Media goes to object storage via presigned upload; a transcoder produces renditions; the CDN serves them. Post stores only the media ids and URLs.

Deletes: soft delete in the post DB, publish post.deleted, workers remove ids from feeds lazily; the hydrator filters tombstoned posts immediately, so the user sees consistent results even if feeds still hold the id. GDPR hard delete is an async job.

Failure modes:

  • Fan-out worker lag: metric is consumer lag; scale workers; the product degrades to slightly older feeds.
  • Redis node down: replica promoted; users on the lost shard rebuilt on demand with throttling.
  • Graph service down: serve cached feed without refresh.
  • Celebrity post spike: hot post cache replicated to local caches (1 to 5 s TTL); CDN for media.

Everyday analogy. Pulling an article from the archive immediately, then slowly removing the clippings from the subscribers' piles.

Common interview traps.

  • Hard deleting and leaving ghost ids that break hydration.
  • No plan for a cold Redis after a restart.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Strategy with numbers: fan-out on write vs read vs hybrid, the celebrity threshold, write amplification (350k inserts/s).
  • Data model: ids only in the feed, Snowflake ids, cursor pagination, cap length.
  • Hydration and counters design; cache hit ratio reasoning.
  • Ranking pipeline basics and latency budget; chronological fallback.
  • Failure and skew: celebrities, hot posts, cache rebuild stampedes, lag.
  • Seniors connect it to storage choices (sharding by author vs id), cost, and the staged evolution seen in the Chirp scaling track.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing only the happy path.
  • Forgetting deletes, blocks and privacy filtering.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Feed = per-user list of post ids. Push (fan-out on write) makes reads cheap; pull makes writes cheap; hybrid uses push for normal authors and pull for celebrities.
  • Numbers: 100k feed reads/s, 350k fan-out inserts/s, about 2 TB of ids in Redis; media goes to CDN.
  • Use Snowflake ids, cursor pagination, ids-only caches, batched hydration, and a rebuild path.
  • Rank in two stages (candidates, model) inside a 200 ms budget, with a chronological fallback.
  • Hot counters need sharded or async counting; deletes are tombstones filtered at hydration.
  • Fan-out through Kafka and workers; protect against lag and stampedes.
